paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy characterized by facial features resembling those of Noonan syndrome together with distinctive ectodermal abnormalities. Mazzanti et al. (2003) described short stature, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, short neck with redundant skin, severe growth hormone (GH) deficiency, mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), darkly pigmented and hairless skin, and loose anagen hair. Cordeddu et al. (2009) added hair that is easily pluckable, sparse, thin and slow growing, cardiac anomalies with overrepresentation of mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects, and a characteristically hypernasal voice.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) reviewed the clinical features of 25 individuals carrying a SHOC2 mutation and found a consistent phenotype. Facial features seemed typical for Noonan syndrome; common features included macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set/posteriorly rotated ears, short and webbed neck, and pectus anomalies. Patients had reduced growth, frequently associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behavior that improved with age in most, and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair. In 12 subjects, loose anagen hair was confirmed by microscopic examination of pulled hairs. Most had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were observed in the majority, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects significantly overrepresented compared with the general Noonan syndrome population, and the voice was characteristically hypernasal. Referring pediatricians had felt that several subjects had features suggestive of Costello syndrome or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome as newborns or young infants.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a de novo SHOC2 ser2-to-gly mutation who presented with fetal distress requiring premature delivery at 32 weeks. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography revealed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction; the cardiac lesion progressed rapidly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors noted that his cardiac findings and features were not typical of those previously reported with this mutation.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 males with the SHOC2 ser2-to-gly mutation. All had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, and developmental delay, and 4 of 4 had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly occurred in 4 of 5, and 3 of 5 had polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, or required a feeding tube. None had been formally diagnosed with loose anagen hair, but all had sparse, very slow-growing hair of unruly texture and unusually light coloring, together with unusually long eyelashes. Four of the 5 patients had been suspected of having Costello syndrome. Brain abnormalities included relative megalencephaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium; cerebellar tonsillar ectopia was present in 3 of 4. One patient (patient 4), whose father was of Mexican ancestry, had periventricular nodular heterotopia and postnatal development of a Chiari I malformation. Patient 1 developed myelofibrosis at age 2 years; bone marrow testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation was negative, and he died at age 2.5 years after splenectomy in preparation for bone marrow transplantation. Patient 3 had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aggressive behavior, and was diagnosed with pervasive developmental disorder and Tourette syndrome at 9 years.

paragraphs.text: Hannig et al. (2014) reported a 5-year-old girl, the oldest child of nonconsanguineous parents of European ancestry, who was referred for right optic nerve hypoplasia, bilateral nystagmus, speech delay, poor hair growth and hyperactive behavior. She had average stature, macrocephaly, sparse and slow-growing hair that was not loose, normal skin pigmentation, bilateral ptosis, wide-spaced nipples, and clubbed nails; MRI showed multiple irregularities of unknown significance in the midbrain, pons and medulla. Her father, who carried the same SHOC2 variant, was 6 feet 3 inches tall and had intellectual disability, a high-arched palate, sparse hair and clubbed nails. Echocardiograms and renal ultrasounds were negative in both. The authors noted that the girl did not have short stature, a cardiac anomaly, hyperpigmentation, ichthyosis or loose anagen hair, and that her features overlapped those of Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome and Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with a RASopathy phenotype overlapping Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome and Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, resulting in a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution in the fourth leucine-rich repeat. Her father, who had sparse hair, clubbed nails and intellectual disability, was also heterozygous. The variant was not found in 6,500 asymptomatic individuals. The mutant protein had impaired interaction with PP1c and could restore only about 10% above basal levels of EGF-induced ERK1/2 activity in SHOC2-depleted cells.

agent.process_note: I read all 11 papers. Cordeddu et al. (2009), Gripp et al. (2013) and Hannig et al. (2014) are full texts and I read them completely. The other eight are abstracts only, and I read each one in full. I used Grep to check zygosity, de novo status and ancestry. No reference data was supplied for the SHOC2 gene, so the intro gives no MIM number or chromosome location for it. None of the papers states that Cordeddu's S2G carriers were heterozygous; heterozygosity is stated only by Hannig et al. (2014) for the M173I variant. The M173I and Q269_H270delinsHY variants are listed as SHOC2 allelic variants, but their phenotypes differ from classic NSLH; the entry describes these differences. PPP1CB (Bertola et al., 2017) is covered only under Heterogeneity. The Motta et al. (2019) abstract gives no zygosity, inheritance or patient demographics.
